Eigenvectors as Equilibrium Conditions

For the past couple of weeks, we have been playing with matrices to model macroscopic phenomena like population dynamics—tracking the transfer of money among major league teams, or modeling the spread of a zombie infestation. There was nothing quantum about it. But what we are going to see over the next few lectures is that quantum mechanics and linear algebra really go hand-in-hand. In fact, linear algebra is the natural language of quantum mechanics.

To ease ourselves into this, let’s ground ourselves with an equation we have seen a lot recently:

\begin{equation} \tag{1} A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v} \end{equation}

We call this our eigenvalue equation. Technically, an eigenvalue equation is a specific, special type of matrix equation. If A is an n \times n matrix (we have mostly looked at 2 \times 2 and 3 \times 3 matrices, but they can easily be 6 \times 6 or larger), then \mathbf{v} must be an n-dimensional vector.

The defining feature of Equation 1 is that the vector \mathbf{v} on the left side and the vector \mathbf{v} on the right side have to be the exact same vector. When a vector survives being multiplied by a matrix without changing its direction, it earns the special title of eigenvector. The scalar multiplier \lambda (the Greek letter lambda) is the eigenvalue. For an n \times n matrix, there are up to n of these eigenvalues, and each one has its own corresponding eigenvector.

Visualizing the Eigendirection

This might seem a little abstract, so let’s bring back our zombie infestation model. We plotted zombies on the vertical axis and humans on the horizontal axis. If you take away anything from the linear algebra unit of this class, let it be this: the eigenvector is a set of numbers that represents an equilibrium condition. It is a state that our system wants to settle into after a long enough time.

I kind of wish people named it an “eigendirection” instead of an eigenvector, because that makes more intuitive sense. Once the system settles into this state, the direction of the vector does not change, even if its overall length does. The behavior of the vector’s length over time is governed entirely by the eigenvalue \lambda:

  • \lambda = 1: The vector stays the exact same length. The population is conserved (no new births or die-offs), and the system has reached a steady state.

  • \lambda > 1: The vector grows. The overall populations are multiplying (e.g., doubling if \lambda = 2), but the ratio of zombies to humans stays the same.

  • \lambda < 1: The vector shrinks. The populations are dying out over time.

  • \lambda < 0: The vector flips back and forth. Every time you take a step in time, the direction of the vector reverses along the same axis.

Suppose our zombie model gives us an eigenvalue of \lambda = 0.8. What physically happens to the human and zombie populations over time?

Because the eigenvalue is less than 1, the state vector shrinks. This means both the human and zombie populations are dying out over time, even though the ratio between them stays constant!

The Schrödinger Equation: Linear Algebra in Disguise

Now, let’s ease into quantum mechanics. Some of you might have heard of the Schrödinger equation in an intro physics or chemistry class. Even if you haven’t, that is perfectly fine—we are going to approach it from scratch.

In a nutshell, the Schrödinger equation—the bread-and-butter equation that runs everything in quantum mechanics—is really just a type of eigenvalue equation.

\begin{equation} \tag{2} \hat{H} |\psi\rangle = E |\psi\rangle \end{equation}

Mapping the Terminology

Let’s break down the funky symbols in Equation 2 and see how they map directly onto the linear algebra concepts we already know.

Mapping Linear Algebra to Quantum Mechanics
Concept Linear Algebra Quantum Mechanics (Schrödinger)
The Equation A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v} \hat{H} |\psi\rangle = E |\psi\rangle
The Operator Matrix A Hamiltonian \hat{H} (Energy Operator)
The State Eigenvector \mathbf{v} Quantum State |\psi\rangle (Wave function)
The Scalar Eigenvalue \lambda Energy E

  • \hat{H} (pronounced “H-hat”): This is the Hamiltonian, also known as the energy operator. It acts just like our matrix A. It “does stuff” to the vector. The Hamiltonian contains the physical information about how electrons behave in our specific system.

  • |\psi\rangle (pronounced “ket psi”): This is the quantum state. You might also hear it called the wave function, or the eigenstate. This acts just like our eigenvector \mathbf{v}. The brackets around the Greek letter \psi are called Dirac notation, or “bra-ket” notation, which is standard in quantum mechanics.

  • E: This is the energy, or the energy eigenvalue. This acts just like our eigenvalue \lambda.

If the Hamiltonian \hat{H} acts as our matrix and |\psi\rangle is our eigenvector, what physical property does the eigenvalue represent in a quantum system?

The eigenvalue represents the allowed energy E of that specific quantum state. Just like \lambda scales our eigenvector in macroscopic models, the energy E scales the wave function |\psi\rangle in the Schrödinger equation.

The Matrix Representation

Because the Schrödinger equation is an eigenvalue equation, we can write it out using the exact same matrix mechanics we have been practicing. For a simple molecule with just two atoms and two electrons, the Hamiltonian can be written as a 2 \times 2 matrix, and the quantum state as a 2D vector:

Accuracy Note

Possible error: The matrix size is set by the number of basis states, here one orbital per atom, not by the number of electrons. The notes treat it in a single-electron picture, so the "two electrons" is misleading.

Correction: A two-atom model with one basis orbital per atom gives a 2 \times 2 Hamiltonian for a single electron.

\begin{equation} \tag{3} \begin{pmatrix} E_{11} & E_{12} \\ E_{12} & E_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = E \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Here, the Hamiltonian matrix contains energy terms (E_{11}, E_{12}, etc.) that we either guess or derive from experiments. The quantum state |\psi\rangle is represented by the column vector containing components c_1 and c_2.

Depending on how big your system is—say, a large organic molecule—this matrix can easily be 6 \times 6, or well into the hundreds, thousands, or even millions. A giant matrix means you will have a whole bunch of possible energy eigenvalues (E), and each of those energies will have its own unique eigenstate (|\psi\rangle). We usually care about multiple states, which is why we refer to them as eigenstates (plural).

Note: While we will focus heavily on the matrix representation in this class, you might have seen the Schrödinger equation written as a differential equation in other physics courses. In that context, the Hamiltonian operator \hat{H} takes the form of a differential operator (like -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + V(x)), and the quantum state |\psi\rangle is written as a continuous function \psi(x). Regardless of whether you use matrices or differential equations, the underlying eigenvalue logic remains exactly the same.

Why Do We Care? The Physics Behind the Math

Why do we torture ourselves with this equation? What is in it for us? There are two massive reasons we care about solving the Schrödinger equation.

Allowed Energy Values

First, and most importantly, solving this equation tells us the allowed energy values (E) of the electrons in a material.

Why do we care about electrons? Because they are the fundamental physical building blocks of matter. Electrical, optical, magnetic, chemical, and even mechanical properties all fundamentally derive from how electrons behave in a material. We typically treat this using a “single electron approach,” looking at one electron at a time.

If we can accurately model the allowed energy levels of these electrons, we essentially know everything about the material. And if we know everything about the material, we can engineer it to our liking. There is a massive scientific endeavor in computational materials science dedicated entirely to building better tools to solve for these energy eigenvalues.

Shapes of the Wave Function

Second, solving the equation tells us the allowed “shapes” of the wave function (|\psi\rangle). In other words, where is the electron most likely located?

Let’s picture a simple two-atom system. The positively charged atomic nuclei are fixed in place, and the electrons are buzzing around them. The Schrödinger equation reveals different ways these electrons can arrange themselves:

  • Localized electrons: The electrons might tend to stick close to their respective nuclei. They are localized, buzzing around in a cloud right where the nuclei are. For those of you who like chemistry, this corresponds to an anti-bonding molecular orbital.

  • Delocalized electrons: The electrons have other choices. They might spread out, orbiting around both nuclei collectively and being shared between them. In chemistry terms, this corresponds to a bonding molecular orbital.

If we solve the Schrödinger equation for a two-atom system and find a wave function where the electrons are shared collectively between both nuclei, what kind of chemical orbital have we found?

You have found a bonding molecular orbital! This occurs because the electrons are delocalized, meaning they spread out and are shared between both nuclei rather than being stuck to just one.

By solving for the eigenstates |\psi\rangle, we get a direct look at these wave function shapes, giving us profound insights into how atoms bond and interact. Next week, we will start putting actual numbers into these matrices and playing with the equation ourselves.
